about: I'm a consultant, a coach and a father, based in Hobart. My weeks are spent inside other people's problems — reading the room, running the project, trying to leave things better than I found them. Every Sunday I write one short essay about what that's actually like, at work and at home.
aboutMore: The consulting is projects — the kind of system change that touches every person in an organisation, where the real risk is never the software. The coaching is leadership teams and the people in them: the conversation nobody's having, and what it's costing them. And for over a decade I've been teaching people how to run their inbox and protect the work that actually matters.

Most of what I write comes out of something that happened that week. A moment in a meeting I couldn't stop thinking about, a habit I caught myself in, a thing I got wrong and only noticed later. I'm usually somewhere in the story, and not often as the person who had it sorted.
The thread running through all of it is the difference between what happens by default and what only happens because someone decided it would. Nothing worth having happens by default.

Some weeks that's a project, a client, or the person you're meant to be handing the work to. Other weeks it's my two daughters, and what I've handed on to them without ever deciding to. I've stopped trying to keep those separate, because the same thing is going on in both.
